newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS says world markets calm, maybe vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: BIS says world markets calm, maybe vulnerable.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said on Thursday world financial markets were relatively calm in the third quarter of 1996, but that a rush into higher risk securities could leave markets exposed.
In a quarterly report on world markets, the BIS -- central bank to the world's major central banks -- also said optimism was growing that the European Union single currency plan would succeed.
It said net issues of new international bonds and euronotes from July through September totalled $101.0 billion, slightly below the previous quarter but 30 percent ahead of the year-ago figure.

"World financial markets in the third quarter of 1996 were characterised by a relatively calm climate, as well as growing optimism concerning the implementation of European economic and monetary union (EMU) and the economic outlook in developing countries," the report said.

International diversification of portfolios was accelerating as new borrowers, new currencies and new instruments were drawn to markets by currency stability late in the third quarter, high liquidity and continued low inflation.

But the growing volume of securities financing and lower-rated or unrated issues was raising questions about the stability of market flows, risk pricing, transparancy of financial instruments and liquidity of lower-rated or complex issues.
"Indeed, concerns have been expressed that the prevailing mood of euphoria might leave markets somewhat exposed," the BIS said.

"Attention has been focused in particular on the growing preference for risky debt, which might be abruptly reversed by a turn in the interest rate cycle in the major economies, and on unresolved issues relating to the practical implementation of EMU," it said.
On the banking market, the BIS said new international syndicated loans almost halved in the third quarter to $69.3 billion from a record $135.5 billion in the second quarter.

But the downturn did not necessarily mean an end to recent market bouyancy because the second quarter's high level resulted mainly from loans to finance U.S. mergers and acquisitions and the French social security system, the BIS said.
It said borrowers from industrial countries accounted for the bulk of bank lending but there was some increase in emerging markets.

"The strong liquidity positions of banks stimulated their appetite for lower-rated names, leading to a further narrowing of margins for eastern European signatures, although this was offset by the entry of high-margin borrowers from the developing world," the report said.

It said a growing role in international shoter-term credit was played by repurchase agreements, or repos, under which a borrower sells a security to a lender for cash with an agreement to buy back the security at a fixed time or price.
The BIS said statistics for international repos were not directly available but estimated that securities underlying repo transactions on the world market totalled at least $1 trillion .

"When seen in relation to more than $9 trillion and nearly $5 trillion of gross and net international bank credit outstanding at mid-1996, the role of repos in the international banking market therefore appears significant."
